sentences.grammar: ‘If + past (meant), would + verb (send)’ talks about an imagined case, not a real one; ‘was just going to say’ means was about to say; ‘as you call him’ is an extra remark between commas.

sentences.context: and when at last he got somewhere near the thing he was trying to
sentences.simple: When he had come up, he at last got somewhere near the thing he was trying to catch. But it floated away from him until it, too, got under the waterfall and was forced down to the bottom.
sentences.grammar: ‘The thing he was trying to catch’ has no ‘that’: the thing is the object of ‘catch’, so ‘that’ can be left out; ‘was forced down’ is passive (the water did it).

sentences.context: But if someone who had never seen a lion looked at Puzzle in his
sentences.simple: Someone who had never seen a lion might think Puzzle in his lion-skin was a lion. This could happen if he did not come too close, if the light was not too good, and if Puzzle did not bray or make any noise with his hoofs.
sentences.grammar: ‘Someone who had never seen a lion’ is a ‘who’ clause in the past perfect; ‘might mistake X for Y’ means might wrongly think X is Y; each ‘if + didn’t ...’ is one condition that must be true.

sentences.context: He was so old that no one could remember when he had first come
sentences.simple: He was so old that no one could remember when he had first come to live in those parts. He was the cleverest, ugliest, most wrinkled Ape you can imagine.
sentences.grammar: ‘So old that’ shows a result; ‘had first come’ (past perfect) is a time before ‘could remember’; ‘the cleverest, ugliest, most wrinkled’ are superlatives (the most of all).

sentences.context: Roonwit had just raised his hand and was leaning forward
sentences.simple: Roonwit had just lifted his hand and was leaning forward to say something very seriously to the King. Then all three of them turned their heads to listen to a wailing sound that was quickly coming nearer.
sentences.grammar: ‘had just raised’ (past perfect) is the earlier action; ‘was leaning’ and ‘was quickly drawing nearer’ show things going on when the next event came.

sentences.context: Up till now Tirian had taken it for granted that the horses
sentences.simple: Until now, Tirian had taken it for granted that the horses the Calormenes were driving were their own horses. He had thought they were dumb animals with no sense, like the horses of our own world.
sentences.grammar: ‘Take it for granted that ...’ means believe something is true without asking; ‘had taken’ (past perfect) shows he believed it until ‘up till now’.

sentences.context: that forest where the trees of gold and of silver had once grown
sentences.simple: Right through the middle of that old forest, a wide lane had already been opened. It was the forest where trees of gold and of silver had once grown and where a child from our world had once planted the Tree of Protection.
sentences.grammar: ‘Where ... had once grown’ and ‘had once planted’ (past perfect) are things from long before; ‘had already been opened’ is passive past perfect (done before, no doer named).

sentences.context: If he had been allowed to speak, the rule of the Ape might have
sentences.simple: If he had been allowed to speak, the rule of the Ape might have ended that day. The Beasts might have seen the truth and thrown the Ape down.
sentences.grammar: ‘If + had been allowed (passive past perfect), might have ended’ is about the past that did not happen: he was not allowed to speak, so the rule did not end.

sentences.context: He had been staring hard at the Ape and the Calormene captain
sentences.simple: He had been staring hard at the Ape and the Calormene captain all the time. He had never once blinked his eyes.
sentences.grammar: ‘Had been staring’ (past perfect continuous) shows he had kept doing it for some time up to that moment; ‘never once’ is a strong ‘not at all’.

sentences.context: He had jeweled slippers on his hind paws which would not stay on properly
sentences.simple: He had slippers with jewels on his back feet. They would not stay on properly, because, as you know, the back feet of an Ape are really like hands.
sentences.grammar: ‘Which would not stay on’ is a ‘which’ clause about the slippers; ‘would not’ here means they failed to stay on (past of ‘won’t’); ‘because’ gives the reason.

sentences.context: He who sat at the right hand of the old man was hardly full
sentences.simple: The one who sat on the right of the old man was not quite fully grown. He was younger than Tirian himself, but his face already had the look of a king and a warrior.
sentences.grammar: ‘He who’ is old-fashioned for ‘the one who’; ‘hardly full grown’ means only just not fully grown; ‘had already the look of’ is old word order for ‘already had the look of’.

sentences.context: If it was only the Ape and the Calormenes who were against you
sentences.simple: If it was only the Ape and the Calormenes who were against you, we would have fought until we were cut to pieces, before we let them tie you up.
sentences.grammar: ‘If it was only A and B who ...’ uses the ‘it was ... who’ pattern to point to A and B; ‘would have fought ... before we’d have let’ says what they would have done: fight to the end rather than let them.

sentences.context: Both these were carrying little bags on their backs which gave them a curious
sentences.simple: Both of them had small bags on their backs. In the dark, the bags made them look strange. At first he wondered what animals they were.
sentences.grammar: ‘Which gave them a curious look’ is a ‘which’ clause about the little bags; ‘so that at first he wondered ...’ shows the result.

sentences.context: The wood in front of him had been quite empty a second before
sentences.simple: A second before, the wood in front of him had been quite empty. He knew they had not come from behind his tree, for he would have heard them.
sentences.grammar: ‘Had been’ (past perfect) is for what was true earlier; ‘would have heard’ says what would have happened if they had come that way; ‘for’ here means ‘because’.

sentences.context: a wooden staircase in one corner led up to a trap door
sentences.simple: There was only one room in it, and this room went right up to the stone roof. A wooden staircase in one corner led up to a trap door, a small door in the roof. Through it you could get out onto the battlements, the top of the wall.
sentences.grammar: ‘By which you could get out’ uses ‘by which’ to mean ‘through which’ (the trap door); ‘you’ means people in general; ‘a trap door by which ...’ is a relative clause.

sentences.context: After that, if they succeeded, they would try to get away Eastward
sentences.simple: After that, if they succeeded, they would try to get away to the east. They would meet the little army that Roonwit the Centaur would be bringing from Cair Paravel.
sentences.grammar: ‘If they succeeded, they would try’ is a possible future seen from the past; ‘would be bringing’ is something expected to be going on at that later time.

sentences.context: The others obeyed at once for they had already lingered long enough
sentences.simple: The others did what he said at once, for they had already stayed long enough in that dangerous place, and the Dwarf drums seemed to have come a little nearer.
sentences.grammar: ‘For’ here means ‘because’; ‘had already lingered’ (past perfect) says they had stayed before this moment; ‘seemed to have come’ means it looked as if the drums had moved nearer.

sentences.context: First, he had given Jill some practice in archery
sentences.simple: First he had given Jill some practice with the bow. He found that, though she was not up to Narnian standards, she was really not too bad.
sentences.grammar: ‘Though not up to Narnian standards’ is a short ‘though’ phrase with no verb (‘she was’ is left out); ‘not up to’ means not as good as; it adds a contrast to ‘not too bad’.

sentences.context: One of those dreadful midnight meetings had just broken up the night before last
sentences.simple: One of those dreadful midnight meetings had just broken up the night before last. I had gone a bit of the way home when I found I had left my pipe behind.
sentences.grammar: ‘Had just broken up’ and ‘I’d left’ (past perfect) show what came before the other past event; ‘break up’ means end.

sentences.context: While the meal was cooking—which seemed a very long time
sentences.simple: While the meal was cooking, which seemed a very long time because it smelled nicer and nicer as it got nearer to being done, the King found a whole Dwarf outfit for Poggin: mail shirt, helmet, shield, sword, belt and dagger.
sentences.grammar: ‘Which seemed a very long time’ is a ‘which’ clause about the whole cooking time, set between dashes; ‘nicer and nicer’ shows something growing; ‘the nearer it came’ means as it came closer.

sentences.context: He had been kicked (he’d done some kicking back too) and beaten
sentences.simple: He had been kicked and beaten. He had done some kicking back too. They had threatened to kill him unless he would say that he believed it was Aslan who was brought out and shown to them by firelight every night.
sentences.grammar: ‘Had been kicked ... and beaten and threatened’ is passive past perfect (the doers are not named); ‘unless he would say’ means if he would not say.

sentences.context: who had lived before the days of the White Witch and the Great Winter
sentences.simple: He spoke of Swanwhite the Queen, who had lived before the days of the White Witch and the Great Winter. She was so beautiful that when she looked into any forest pool, the reflection of her face shone out of the water like a star by night for a year and a day afterward.
sentences.grammar: ‘Who had lived before’ is a past perfect ‘who’ clause (she lived earlier than the story); ‘so beautiful that’ shows a result.

sentences.context: When Tirian realized that the two strangers could not get home
sentences.simple: When Tirian realized that the two strangers could not get home (unless Aslan suddenly took them away), he next wanted them to go across the Southern mountains into Archenland, where they might possibly be safe.
sentences.grammar: ‘Unless’ means ‘if not’; ‘where they might possibly be safe’ is a ‘where’ clause about Archenland; ‘realized that ...’ is followed by a noun clause.

sentences.context: What was the good, now, of telling the Beasts that an ass had been
sentences.simple: What was the use of telling the Beasts that someone had dressed an ass as a lion to trick them?
sentences.grammar: ‘an ass had been dressed up’ is passive past perfect: we know what was done, not who did it; ‘What was the good of + -ing’ means it was no use.

sentences.context: they would have seen him at once if they had looked in the right
sentences.simple: They were going toward the bonfire and were close to Tirian. They would have seen him at once if they had looked the right way.
sentences.grammar: ‘would have seen ... if they had looked’ is a past ‘if’ sentence: they did not look, so they did not see him.

sentences.context: Ginger the Cat said in a cool, clear voice, not at all as if
sentences.simple: Ginger the Cat said in a cool, clear voice, not at all as if he was excited, ‘I will go in, if you like.’
sentences.grammar: ‘Not at all as if he was excited’ tells how he sounded: calm, not excited; ‘I’ll go in, if you like’ offers to do something, with ‘if you like’ meaning ‘if you want’.

sentences.context: He had never seen anything (though he had seen both a dragon and a
sentences.simple: He had never seen anything that made his blood run so cold as that line of dark-faced, bright-eyed men, though he had seen both a dragon and a sea serpent.
sentences.grammar: ‘Had never seen’ and ‘had seen’ (past perfect) compare this moment with his earlier life; ‘made his blood run cold’ means frightened very much; ‘so cold as’ compares; ‘though’ adds a contrast.

sentences.context: They had just begun to hope that they might win that night
sentences.simple: They had just started to hope that they might win that night. But it would be all over with them if new enemies appeared.
sentences.grammar: ‘Had just begun to hope’ (past perfect) is the earlier action; ‘it would be all over with them if ...’ is an ‘if’ sentence about a possible danger; ‘all over with’ means finished.

sentences.context: when the eleven Dwarfs, one after the other, had been flung or kicked
sentences.simple: When the eleven Dwarfs, one after the other, had been thrown or kicked into that dark doorway, and the door had been shut again, he bowed low to the stable and said:
sentences.grammar: ‘had been flung or kicked’ and ‘had been shut’ are passive past perfect: these things were done first, then he bowed.

sentences.context: He remembered everything now, and he realized that the enemy had been edging him
sentences.simple: He remembered everything now, and he realized that the enemy had been slowly moving him to the stable on purpose ever since the fight began.
sentences.grammar: ‘Had been edging him ... ever since the fight began’ (past perfect continuous) shows an action that went on up to the moment he understood; ‘on purpose’ means not by chance.

sentences.context: although the cords with which they had been tied seemed to have vanished
sentences.simple: They were not walking about or enjoying themselves, although the cords that had tied them seemed to be gone. They were not lying down and having a rest either.
sentences.grammar: ‘With which they had been tied’ is a passive past perfect clause with ‘with which’ (formal for ‘that they had been tied with’); ‘seemed to have vanished’ means it looked as if they had gone; ‘nor were they’ puts ‘were’ before ‘they’ after ‘nor’.

sentences.context: Then the Dwarfs all cocked their heads as if they couldn’t see anyone
sentences.simple: Then all the Dwarfs turned their heads to one side, as if they could not see anyone. They seemed to listen hard and try to guess from the sound what was happening.
sentences.grammar: ‘as if they couldn’t see’ tells how it looked, not what is true; ‘what was happening’ is a clause that is the object of ‘guess’.

sentences.context: unless either the Door had grown very much larger
sentences.simple: Obviously, unless either the Door had grown very much larger or the creatures had suddenly become as small as gnats (tiny flying insects), a crowd like that could not ever have tried to get through it.
sentences.grammar: ‘Unless ... had grown’ (past perfect) means ‘if it had not grown’; ‘either ... or’ gives two ways it could have been possible; ‘couldn’t ever have tried’ says it was not possible.

sentences.context: you could see all sorts of things about its shape
sentences.simple: The whole country became bare, and you could see all sorts of things about its shape, all the little bumps and low places, which you had never noticed before.
sentences.grammar: ‘Which you had never noticed before’ (past perfect) says you had not seen these things earlier; ‘all sorts of things’ means many different things.

sentences.context: Not because he and I are one, but because we are opposites
sentences.simple: It is not because he and I are one, but because we are opposites, that I take to me the services you have done to him.
sentences.grammar: ‘Not because A, but because B’ says the true reason is B; ‘I take to me’ is old style for ‘I take as mine’; ‘thou hast done’ is old style for ‘you have done’.

sentences.context: Everyone else began to run, and they found, to their astonishment
sentences.simple: Everyone else began to run, and they found, to their surprise, that they could keep up with him. Even fat little Puzzle and short-legged Poggin could.
sentences.grammar: ‘Found, to their astonishment, that they could keep up with him’ is ‘find + that-clause’ with an added phrase; ‘not only ... but even ...’ stresses that even the slowest could do it; ‘keep up with’ means go as fast as someone.

sentences.context: They were out of Narnia now and up into the Western Wild
sentences.simple: They were out of Narnia now and up into the Western Wild, which neither Tirian nor Peter nor even the Eagle had ever seen before.
sentences.grammar: ‘Which ... had ever seen before’ is a relative clause where ‘which’ is the object of ‘seen’; ‘neither ... nor ... nor even’ joins the three; past perfect says none had seen it before.

sentences.context: not as Tirian had seen him last when they brought him home pale and
sentences.simple: It was his own father, the good King Erlian. But he was not as Tirian had seen him last, when they brought him home pale and wounded from his fight with the giant. And he was not as Tirian remembered him in his later years, when he was a gray-headed warrior.
sentences.grammar: ‘Not as Tirian had seen him last’ means not as he looked the last time Tirian saw him (past perfect = earlier); ‘nor even as’ adds a second ‘not like’ picture.

sentences.context: the very first person whom Aslan called to him was Puzzle the Donkey
sentences.simple: And the very first person whom Aslan called to him was Puzzle the Donkey.
sentences.grammar: ‘Whom Aslan called to him’ is a relative clause with ‘whom’ (formal, as the object); ‘the very first’ stresses ‘first’; ‘called to him’ means asked to come to him.
